title: Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost
gist: Hugging Face shows that RL-training a LoRA 'harness adapter' for Qwen3.8-27B inside each agent harness (pi, OpenCode, Hermes Agent) lifts SWE-bench Pro and Terminal-Bench 2.1 pass@1 by up to ~25 points while cutting tool calls and tokens by roughly half or more. It open-sources the full recipe (curated RL coding tasks, TRL AsyncGRPOTrainer, OpenEnv/Harbor) and a merged super-adapter that works across all three harnesses, while flagging 'reasoning leakage' as an open question.

insights.claim: Hugging Face argues general-purpose LLMs are not optimized for any specific agent harness or task mix, so pairing a model with a harness leaves accuracy and efficiency unrealized that a custom RL-trained LoRA 'harness adapter' can recover.
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: Points to a post-training/customization layer (per-harness adapters) as a value-capture spot for open-weight model users and tooling vendors.
insights.quote: Models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance.

insights.claim: Adding a frozen-weights RL-trained LoRA adapter to Qwen3.8-27B under the pi harness lifted Terminal-Bench 2.1 pass@1 from 39% to 55% while cutting average token use per task from 2.9K to 1.5K.
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: Cheap adapters can roughly halve inference tokens while improving accuracy — a direct cost lever for agentic coding deployments on open models.

insights.claim: Hugging Face attributes most of the harness-adapter gain to the model reasoning less, calling fewer tools, and succeeding on the first attempt rather than to new raw capability.
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: Efficiency gains (fewer tool calls/tokens) are the main mechanism, implying lower serving cost per solved task.
insights.quote: Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time.

insights.claim: Unlike most RL frameworks (verl, SkyRL-Gym, rLLM, slime, ART) that train on a re-implemented agent loop, Hugging Face's recipe runs the harness exactly as shipped and trains on the exact tokens recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM, a direction also taken by Agent Lightning v1.0 and SkyRL's Harbor integration.
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: 'Harnessed agentic RL' is becoming an industry pattern; watch for RL tooling that trains on production harness traces rather than framework abstractions.
insights.quote: Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM.

insights.claim: Hugging Face trained one LoRA adapter for Qwen3.8-27B per harness (Pi 1.5.2, OpenCode 2.2.7, Hermes Agent v0.22.6), with datasets, training and rollouts all running on Hugging Face Jobs using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, OpenEnv and Harbor, and released all artifacts openly.
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: Hugging Face is positioning its Hub/Jobs stack as an end-to-end RL platform, a strategic move up the stack from model hosting.

insights.claim: A broad Hub search found about 59,000 Harbor-format RL tasks, but duplicates, evaluation sets and not-for-training tasks meant Hugging Face kept only two Hub sources (SWE-smith and SWE-Gym via TaskTrove) plus a third set generated with Tasksmith from Repo2RLEnv.
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: Raw volume of public RL environments overstates usable training data; curation and contamination control are the bottleneck.

insights.claim: RL training requires a verifier proven correct, because a verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches wrong behavior, and tasks the model already solves teach nothing.
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: Verified environment/task quality is a key moat for RL data vendors and labs.
insights.quote: A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior.
insights.locator: Generating custom RL tasks on Hugging Face

insights.claim: Only 858 of 1,127 Hub candidate tasks passed openenv validate's semantic checks, and wrong-answer controls exposed defects including a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers.
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: Even published benchmark verifiers can be broken — reported agentic benchmark scores deserve skepticism.

insights.claim: Tasksmith produced 24 validated tasks across 10 Python repositories from 30 merged pull requests, targeting skill gaps such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization mapped from Terminal-Bench 2.1, SWE-bench Pro hard and DeepSWE.
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: Synthetic task generation from real PRs offers a scalable path to targeted RL data for any codebase.
insights.locator: We used Tasksmith to target gaps.

insights.claim: Because GRPO scores each attempt relative to others on the same task, tasks the base model always or never solves provide no learning signal; of 442 scored tasks Qwen3.8-27B solved 151 every time and 120 never, leaving 171 'qualified' tasks.
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: Difficulty filtering throws away most of the data — usable RL signal is scarce and model-specific, raising the value of fresh task generation.
insights.quote: A valid task can still teach nothing.
insights.locator: Difficulty check with the base model

insights.claim: The released harness-hub/agentic-coding-envs dataset holds 871 tasks from 35 repositories (717 SWE-smith, 130 SWE-Gym, 24 Tasksmith), of which 171 are qualified for GRPO, with Hub tasks capped at 40 per repository.
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: Open, reusable RL coding environments lower the barrier for third parties to fine-tune agentic models.

insights.claim: A learning-rate sweep found 1e-5 barely moved correctness, 1e-4 collapsed rollouts (turns per rollout fell from 18 to 6 with rising entropy), and 5e-5 improved correctness from 0.49 to 0.60 by step 40 but became unstable over longer runs, so final runs used 2e-5.
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: Agentic RL on LoRA is fragile and hyperparameter-sensitive; reproducibility for smaller teams is non-trivial.
insights.locator: We performed a small LR sweep

insights.claim: The reward combined verifier correctness with a small 0.1 tool-efficiency bonus, and thinking mode was turned off during rollouts to maximize training efficiency.
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: Explicitly rewarding tool efficiency is a design choice that drives the observed token/cost savings.

insights.claim: Each harness adapter trained on just two NVIDIA B200 GPUs (one for the vLLM server, one for training), and as the model improved more task groups fit into each step's token budget, diversifying the learning signal.
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: Harness adaptation of a 27B model is feasible on a 2-GPU budget — democratizing custom agent post-training.

insights.claim: Total training ran 598 cumulative steps over 78,114 samples and 167M trained tokens; training correctness stayed roughly flat while trajectories shortened and groups per step more than doubled, with gains appearing on held-out benchmarks.
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: Flat training reward can mask real held-out improvement in agentic RL — evaluate on held-out sets, not reward curves.

insights.claim: The safeagents plugin checked 1.3M tool calls across the three training runs and blocked 647 suspicious ones, with blocked calls per 1,000 declining over training.
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: Guardrail tooling for reward-hacking/misbehavior during RL is becoming a standard component of the training stack.

insights.claim: The three harness LoRA adapters' weight updates had pairwise cosine similarity of only about 0.01–0.02, meaning each harness pushed the model in a nearly orthogonal direction, the best case for merging.
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: Harness-specific skills are largely non-interfering, so one model can cheaply serve multiple harnesses via merged adapters.
insights.locator: Super-adapter: merging all adapters into one

insights.claim: Merging adapters by rank concatenation at weight ½ gave the best balance (52.5% across harnesses on Terminal-Bench 2.1 vs 43.3% base, 25.9 tool calls vs 49.2), while the plain sum over-applied updates and pushed pi back to base-level accuracy.
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: Merge weighting matters; sub-unit scaling (consistent with task arithmetic/TIES/KnOTS literature) is the practical default.
insights.quote: The plain sum over-applies the updates.

insights.claim: With thinking off, the super-adapter improved on base Qwen3.8-27B on all six harness–benchmark pairs (mean pass@1 39.5% to 49.0%; 71 tasks newly solved vs 34 lost, p < 0.001).
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: A single general adapter delivers a ~10-point lift across harnesses with no harness-specific deployment.
insights.locator: With thinking off, the super-adapter improves

insights.claim: Despite never being trained with thinking on, the super-adapter was the strongest model Hugging Face evaluated in thinking mode, beating the base model at the same effort on five of six pairs (mean 55.5% to 63.5%), with gains of +16 points under Hermes and +20 under OpenCode on SWE-bench Pro.
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: Non-thinking RL can transfer to thinking mode — suggests cheaper training regimes may still lift reasoning-mode performance.
insights.quote: Despite not being trained at all with thinking on, it's the strongest model we evaluated with thinking mode.
insights.locator: Despite not being trained at all with thinking on

insights.claim: Specialist harness adapters remain better than the super-adapter with thinking off on four of six pairs, most under pi (64.0% vs 46.0% on SWE-bench Pro), so single-harness users should prefer the specialist.
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: Merging has a real accuracy cost for some harnesses; deployment choice depends on harness diversity.
insights.quote: If you only use one harness and keep thinking off, take its specialist.
insights.locator: Use the specialist harness adapters when thinking off.

insights.claim: On tasks solved by both base and super-adapter with thinking off, the super-adapter made 53–73% fewer tool calls and 44–60% fewer tokens per task; with thinking on it still cut tool calls 31–48% and tokens 24–43% on SWE-bench Pro.
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: Large inference-cost reduction for agentic coding on open weights — pressure on per-token pricing economics of closed agent models.
insights.locator: The super adapter is also much more efficient.

insights.claim: Hugging Face cautions that the ½ merge weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with step-120 adapters, so its Terminal-Bench numbers are slightly optimistic, whereas SWE-bench Pro played no part in the choice.
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: Weight SWE-bench Pro results more heavily when assessing the super-adapter.
insights.locator: The ½ weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench 2.1

insights.claim: Under its own harness on the 51 hardest SWE-bench Pro tasks, the pi adapter rose from 39.2% to 64.7% (+25.5 points, p = 0.002), Hermes from 29.4% to 43.1%, and OpenCode from 35.3% to 51.0%.
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: Double-digit gains on hard real-world SWE tasks from a LoRA narrow the gap between open 27B models and larger proprietary agents.

insights.claim: On the full Terminal-Bench 2.1, pi gained +16.3 points and Hermes +14.1, while OpenCode gained +6.0 overall and +13.6 on the 66 tasks not used for checkpoint selection; adapters cut tool calls 56–72% on SWE-bench Pro and 53–70% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 on commonly solved tasks.
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: Consistent accuracy-plus-efficiency wins across harnesses strengthen the case for per-harness post-training.

insights.claim: Results cannot be compared across harnesses because default settings differ, e.g. Pi does not keep previous reasoning turns while OpenCode and Hermes do, which drives rapid context overflow on SWE-bench Pro.
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: Harness design choices materially swing agent benchmark scores, so cross-harness leaderboards are apples-to-oranges.
insights.quote: using Pi does not necessarily lead to better results than Hermes or OpenCode

insights.claim: The pi-trained adapter transferred to other harnesses: under OpenCode it matched OpenCode's own specialist on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (44.8% to 54.0%) and under Hermes kept about two-thirds of the specialist's gain, with a similar ~45% tool-call cut.
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: Learned agentic efficiency is partly harness-agnostic, increasing the reusability of a single adapter.
insights.quote: Therefore it seems that the newly learned capabilities are transferred across harnesses.
insights.locator: Does the efficiency and performance ability transfer across harnesses?

insights.claim: On 300 out-of-distribution AutomationBench business-automation tasks run in AutomationBench's own agent loop, adapters stayed close to base (pi 27.0%, OpenCode 25.3%, merged 23.7% vs base 23.0%; Hermes 17.7%), so harness RL neither clearly transferred nor broke the model.
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: Harness adapters are domain-specific; don't expect gains outside SWE-style tasks, though catastrophic regression appears limited (Hermes a possible exception).
insights.locator: Evaluation on out-of-distribution tasks and setup

insights.claim: Post-release trajectory inspection showed the adapted model in non-thinking mode emits short reasoning-like text (e.g. 'wait', 'let me see') before tool calls, which Hugging Face calls 'reasoning leakage' — the model learning to escape non-thinking mode toward thinking behavior.
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: Part of the non-thinking gain may be implicit reasoning, complicating claims of pure efficiency gains and highlighting RL's tendency to find unintended strategies.
insights.quote: This phenomenon can be seen as a sort of ‘reasoning leakage’
insights.locator: Open question: What did the model really learn to do?

insights.claim: Hugging Face maintains its results remain valid because under a fixed token budget the adapters far outperform the base non-thinking model and match the thinking version while using far fewer tokens.
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: Token-budget-normalized comparisons are the right lens for agent cost/performance claims.

insights.claim: Community users reported the harness adapters also work well on Qwen3.8 derivatives such as Swift-1.5, an unexpected cross-model portability result.
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: Adapters may be portable across fine-tuned derivatives of a base model family, widening their addressable ecosystem.
insights.locator: We appreciate the feedback from the users

insights.claim: Hugging Face plans follow-up work applying the pipeline to pure thinking models and hybrid thinking/non-thinking training, and to more models, and invites builders to create harness adapters from their own codebases.
insights.speaker: Younes B
insights.so_what: Expect a growing ecosystem of community harness adapters on the Hub — a potential distribution/network effect for Hugging Face.
